claims.text: Selective dealloying of a precursor noble metal–based high-entropy alloy yields a three-dimensional nanoframework.
The resulting three-dimensional nanoframework enhances catalytic performance.
The proposed precursor is a homogeneous HEA containing catalytically active noble metals and less noble sacrificial metals.
Electrochemical or chemical dealloying preferentially removes the less noble elements.
Ambient or mildly elevated dealloying temperatures can avoid sintering.
Selective dissolution of less noble atoms creates a porous, interconnected framework.
Selective dissolution enriches the resulting framework in noble-metal sites.
Preferential etching of less noble elements leaves behind a robust, high-surface-area nanostructure.
The three-dimensional framework increases the density of active catalytic sites.
The three-dimensional framework improves mass transport.
Increased active-site density and improved mass transport aid catalysis.
The dealloyed NM-HEA will have greater surface area than the untreated alloy.
The dealloyed NM-HEA will have greater catalytic activity than the untreated alloy.
The untreated homogeneous NM-HEA has a smoother and less porous structure than the proposed dealloyed material.
Effective nanoframework formation requires sufficient chemical contrast between noble and sacrificial elements.
Dealloying effectiveness may diminish when alloy composition does not permit selective removal.
Framework collapse during dealloying may diminish the effectiveness of the method.
Dealloying is a well-established method for producing porous noble-metal nanostructures.
Processing conditions and alloy composition strongly influence the resulting framework.
